name: The Difference Principle
statement: Inequalities are just only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.
statementAccent: to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged
meaning: The difference principle is a principle of distributive justice formulated by the American philosopher John Rawls as part of his theory of justice as fairness, set out in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice. It holds that social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they are arranged so as to be of the greatest benefit to the least advantaged members of society. In other words, an unequal distribution of wealth, income, or other goods is just only when it improves the position of the worst-off compared with any more equal alternative; inequality that does not help the least advantaged is unjust. The difference principle is the second part of the second of Rawls's two principles of justice. The first principle guarantees each person an equal claim to a scheme of equal basic liberties, and the second requires that social and economic inequalities be attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. Rawls argued that rational people choosing principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their own place in society, would adopt the difference principle. It became one of the most influential and debated ideas in twentieth-century political philosophy.
mechanism: The difference principle regulates inequality by tying its justification to the situation of the worst-off. Rawls did not demand strict equality; he recognized that some inequalities, such as higher pay to attract people into demanding or productive roles, can make everyone better off, including the least advantaged, by expanding the total output that can be shared. The difference principle sets the test for when such inequalities are acceptable: an inequality is just only if the resulting arrangement leaves the least advantaged group better off than they would be under any alternative arrangement, including a more equal one. If an inequality could be reduced without making the worst-off worse off, or if a different arrangement would benefit them more, then the existing inequality is unjust. This reflects a kind of maximin reasoning, maximizing the minimum, focusing distributive concern on raising the floor rather than on the average or the top. Rawls argued that parties in the original position, choosing principles behind a veil of ignorance that hides their own talents and social position, would reason cautiously and adopt the difference principle, since any of them might turn out to be among the least advantaged. The principle thus links a procedure of fair choice to a substantive standard for judging economic inequality.

examples.text: Higher pay for a demanding role is just under the difference principle only if it ultimately benefits the least advantaged.
The principle focuses distributive concern on improving the position of the worst-off rather than on the average or the top.
Rawls argued that people choosing justice without knowing their own place in society would adopt the difference principle.

variants.name: The two principles of justice

variants.name: Nozick's entitlement critique
variants.text: Robert Nozick's libertarian objection that a patterned principle like the difference principle violates liberty and property rights.

whyItMatters: The difference principle is one of the most influential ideas in modern political philosophy, giving a rigorous and widely discussed answer to the question of when economic inequality is just. By holding that inequalities are acceptable only when they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, Rawls offered a principled middle path between strict equality and unfettered market outcomes, one that permits inequality but harnesses it to the improvement of the worst-off. The principle, and the theory of justice as fairness it belongs to, revived normative political philosophy in the second half of the twentieth century, offered a powerful alternative to utilitarianism, and became the central reference point for debates about distributive justice, the welfare state, and egalitarian liberalism. It reframed how philosophers and policymakers think about fairness, directing attention to the position of the least advantaged as the measure of a just society. The difference principle also provoked influential responses, notably Robert Nozick's libertarian critique, that themselves shaped the field. As Rawls's standard for just inequality, the difference principle is a cornerstone of contemporary thinking about justice.

accept an inequality only if it leaves the least advantaged better off than any alternative would.
ground the principle in what people would choose from behind a veil of ignorance, unaware of their own place.

limits: The difference principle is influential but heavily contested. The libertarian Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia of 1974 that any patterned principle of distribution like it violates individual liberty and property rights, since maintaining a preferred pattern requires continually interfering with people's voluntary transactions, and that justice depends on how holdings actually arose rather than on end-state patterns. Communitarian critics questioned the abstract individualism underlying the theory. There is also debate over whether parties in the original position would really reason by maximin and choose the difference principle, with John Harsanyi arguing they would instead maximize average utility. The precise formulation of Rawls's first principle also changed between the 1971 edition and his later revisions.
misreadings: The difference principle does not demand strict equality; it permits inequalities, but only when they benefit the least advantaged. It is not simply about helping the poor in general but sets a precise test, that the worst-off be better off than under any alternative arrangement. And it is not an uncontested conclusion, since Nozick argued it violates liberty and Harsanyi that people would instead choose average utility, so treating the principle as requiring equality, as vague charity, or as beyond dispute, misreads Rawls's contested standard for just inequality.
origin: A principle of distributive justice formulated by the American philosopher John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, holding that inequalities are just only if they most benefit the least advantaged; a landmark of twentieth-century political philosophy.
